blogs.content: Introducing Ontological Legal Research | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Resources Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Product Updates Introducing Ontological Legal Research Introducing Ontological Legal Research Category Product Updates published Oct 29, 2026 author Team Legora Today, we’re introducing Ontological Legal Research, starting with the United States. It brings comprehensive legal data together with a proprietary ontology that maps how sources connect. This enables the Legora Agent to see the full picture of current law and navigate it with unprecedented accuracy. One of the hardest problems in legal AI AI fails at legal research in critical ways. Fabricated citations are the most visible failure. Even when the sources are real, AI can cite outdated law, misjudge a source’s authority, or find the main rule but miss the exception. It misses the full picture of current law. Fixing this takes two things: comprehensive legal data and a way for the Agent to understand how the law connects. Whatever it takes to get comprehensive data The single most common frustration we hear from customers is that you can't get the best data and the best technology in one product. Legal publishers have comprehensive data but a weaker AI layer. AI providers have advanced technology but not yet comprehensive data for legal research. Too often, the data our clients buy access to is simply not available in the AI platforms they want to use — one prominent publisher CEO recently noted that only 1% of their data was actually available in a partner's platform. So we’re bringing comprehensive legal data into Legora. Primary law is a public asset, but getting hold of it is surprisingly difficult. The challenges vary by jurisdiction and source type. In Germany, only about 3% of case law is digital. In the UK, legislation from official sources is often two to four weeks behind. In the US, the court reporters are printed by publishers who won’t sell a digital copy. We partner wherever it enables us to deliver the best possible user experience, but where a partnership won’t deliver the right quality or coverage, we go directly to the source and get it ourselves: manual requests, physical scanning. Whatever it takes. US case law is one example. The courts are clear that judicial opinions are a public asset (we brought in outside counsel to confirm), but publishers won’t sell a digital feed of citable cases. So we collect slip opinions directly from court websites within 24-48 hours, then get the physical advance sheets and bound volumes within about a week of release. We take the spines off, remove publisher-added material such as headnotes and annotations, then scan them. To get to 99.997% accuracy, three separate people check every word on every page. Our Attorney Editors bring decades of experience at traditional publishers. They map source coverage in each jurisdiction by document type, including required historical coverage and update frequency. Customer requests drive priorities, and our customers' law librarians help audit the comprehensiveness and accuracy of our data. Building a map of current law With the data in place, the second challenge is understanding how the sources connect, and what is current law. US legal sources alone span tens of millions of documents, far more than any AI model can process at once. The model depends on search to select the material it will read. “For legal research, semantic search is like throwing darts blindfolded" - Arvid Winterfeldt, Product Manager, Legal Research The industry standard uses keyword and semantic search to find relevant passages for the model to reason over. “For legal research, semantic search is like throwing darts blindfolded. It picks up opinions that look useful in isolation, but misses critical context. A later decision may have overruled, narrowed, or criticized one of those opinions. blogs.description: An assignment clause decides which contracts move freely when a business reorganizes. See a sample clause, consent and merger rules, and a review table.
blogs.content: Insights When a Business Reorganizes, Each Assignment Clause Decides Which Contracts Move An assignment clause decides which contracts move freely when a business reorganizes. See a sample clause, consent and merger rules, and a review table. by Harvey Team • Nov 3, 2026 An assignment clause says whether a party can transfer its rights or obligations under a contract to someone else, and on what terms. A restrictive version, often called an anti-assignment clause, requires the other party's consent or limits transfers to named exceptions. A change of control clause can extend that restriction to a sale of the party itself. When a business reorganizes, sells a unit, or raises money, those clauses decide which contracts go with the business. Take a hypothetical software company, OpCo, that's moving its payroll analytics product line into a new wholly owned subsidiary, NewCo. The move covers 240 contracts, including customer agreements, supplier contracts, inbound software licenses, and an office lease in San Jose. About a year later, an outside investor plans to buy 30% of NewCo, and a lender plans to extend a credit line secured by NewCo's receivables. Every company, contract count, and clause in this example is hypothetical. OpCo will transfer the contracts directly, so the reorganization is an assignment of contract rights and duties from OpCo to NewCo. The 240 contracts mix services, sales of goods, software licenses, and a lease, and each type follows its own rules. Results turn on each clause's wording and governing law, so counsel confirms each conclusion for the states involved. Sorting 240 contracts by hand means reading the same few clause types again and again. AI changes that step. Harvey's review tables, for example, pull each contract's assignment terms into columns counsel can check against the source, so lawyer time goes to the consents and judgment calls. A Sample Assignment Clause Shows the Six Phrases That Decide a Transfer OpCo's customer form, used in 160 of the 240 contracts, has a contract assignment clause like this hypothetical one, with its six key phrases numbered: "Neither party may assign this Agreement (1) , whether voluntarily, by operation of law (2) , or otherwise, without the other party's prior written consent, which shall not be unreasonably withheld (3) . Either party may assign this Agreement to an Affiliate, or to a successor to the business it relates to, on written notice and without consent (4) . A Change of Control of a party is deemed an assignment (5) . Any attempted assignment in breach of this Section is void (6) ." The table reads each numbered phrase against OpCo's move: Phrase What it can do What it means for OpCo (1) "Assign this Agreement" Reach rights, duties, or both, depending on how the governing law reads it The move delegates OpCo's duties, so the ban reaches it under either reading (2) "By operation of law" Pull a merger into the restriction, depending on the deal structure and the state Doesn't decide a direct transfer, but would matter if NewCo later merged (3) "Shall not be unreasonably withheld" Generally require a reasonable basis to refuse consent outside the carve-outs Matters only if NewCo falls outside the Affiliate carve-out (4) "To an Affiliate... on written notice" Move the contract without consent, if the assignee meets the defined term and notice follows the notice section Decides the reorganization for the 160 contracts on OpCo's form (5) "Change of Control... deemed an assignment" Treat an ownership change as a transfer, measured by the defined term Decides whether the later investment in NewCo counts (6) "Void" In some states, make a noncompliant transfer ineffective instead of a breach that leaves a damages claim Raises the cost of a missed notice or consent The other 80 contracts use different assignment language, so the rules behind each phrase matter. blogs.content: Precedent New York 2026: The conversations defining the future of legal work | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Resources Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Events Precedent New York 2026: The conversations defining the future of legal work Precedent New York 2026: The conversations defining the future of legal work Category Events published Oct 27, 2026 author Team Legora A little over three years ago, Legora didn’t exist. Last week, we welcomed 250 legal leaders to The Guggenheim in New York for Precedent, our flagship global summit. A lot has changed since the last Precedent at London’s Royal Opera House just six months ago. Legora now serves over 2,400 customers in over 80 markets. The energy in the room was something special. Frank Lloyd Wright’s Guggenheim was built by people who refused to accept that things had to look the way they always had. That’s a precedent worth keeping. It felt like the right room to gather the people who spend their days rethinking legal work. Many of them have shaped Legora along the way. “You push us, you challenge us, and you tell us when things need to get better,” said Legora CEO Max Junestrand, “and we do the same for you.” It was a special night. During the evening, we heard Ramp Co-Founder and Co-CEO Eric Glyman share his insights on finance’s AI transition, legal leaders from Salesforce, Venable, and Microsoft talk about what’s working and what’s next. Max Junestrand also took to the stage with a packed set of announcements, updates and the launch of Ontological Legal Research, which he called “the single biggest thing we have ever worked on.” Some key themes emerged from the fireside chats and panels: The industry has graduated from AI 101 Just a couple of years ago, discussions about AI’s impact on the future of legal work might have been theoretical, but as Legora CFO, David Eckstein, observed in his opening remarks, “we are way past that.” Panelists agreed. Salesforce’s Erica Swainson said her team has moved from prompting basics to model selection, and Venable’s Stuart Ingis said that “rather than our lawyers learning the tools, the tools have learned our lawyers.” Revenue upside, not just efficiency, is showing up in the data. Ramp sees AI-forward companies pulling ahead, and with about 1% of U.S. corporate payments flowing through it, it has a better view than most. Glyman said Ramp’s own growth has accelerated even as it scales, and Ingis reported Venable’s most profitable quarter ever. Laying the foundations before you can move fast Microsoft’s Thomas Daemen leads a 178-person legal team supporting a sales organization that must add roughly $50 billion in revenue a year. Adding headcount couldn’t be the answer, he told The L Suite’s Erika Fisher; technology had to be. It took a year just to get Microsoft’s data estate in order before AI could deliver real value. Once it was in place, the payoff was what Daemen called a “canonical win-win-win”: sellers benefit from a lower cost of sales, the legal team can close deals more efficiently, and customers get answers sooner and a smoother contracting process. It has also changed how legal is perceived. Ticketing data often shows that the clause under fire is an engineering or business-model issue, not a legal one, so legal is no longer seen as the “blocker.” Adoption is a people problem, and requires grace. In his chat with Max Junestrand, Glyman said AI isn’t just about adopting new tools but an entirely new way of working, and it requires some grace and space as we learn it. He modeled this by sharing his own first attempts with Claude Code in front of the whole company, and urged leaders to set up IT access and permissions early and to potentially tolerate a “bad month” of spending so teams reach their first “aha” moment sooner. Ingis described Venable’s AI sandbox and the AI plan every practice group was asked to write, while Swainson pointed to internal champions as the way to keep pace. Max Junestrand: legal work

Scaling fast, built to last. Category Legora voices published Oct 23, 2026 author Max Junestrand Three years on we have more than 2,400 customers, and the rule hasn’t changed. Each one made the product better and the economics healthier. That way of working is the main reason we’ve come this far, and a large part of why we can announce a $550 million Series E this week, at an $8.8 billion post-money valuation, led by Atreides Management. Here is how we got here. Who we raised from New investors include Baron Capital, Fidelity Management & Research Company, Glade Brook Capital Partners, and J.P Morgan. We built this round around those who plan to be with us for the long-game, and every major existing investor, the ones who’ve seen us up close, chose to back us again. We raised with significant cash still in the bank. Our growth doesn’t depend on outside capital, but this round lets us go faster. How we run Legora We build on the best frontier models, and don’t train our own general legal model. That was a real debate when we started in 2023. The models were new, and plenty of people said the way to win in legal AI was to fine-tune your own. We didn’t have the money for it, and fine-tuning didn’t seem to work at our scale. Training a new generation of model costs billions, and most of what lawyers needed wasn’t in the model anyway. It was in everything around it: security, privacy, parsing, working with large sets of documents. So we bet on every frontier model and put our effort into making them work for lawyers. Since then a better, cheaper model has arrived every few months. We build boats, not houses: when the models rise, everything we’ve built floats higher. Legora routes each task to the model that does it best, and we only post-train for narrow jobs where frontier models fall short. That bet also made us efficient. We invested early in model routing and benchmarking. Every new model goes through our own evaluations before it touches customer work, so we know exactly where it’s strong, and each task goes to the model that does it best. Customers get better performance at lower cost, and Legora has always run at a positive gross margin, one that keeps improving. We build Legora together with our customers, and we wanted our pricing to reflect that. We get paid when customers get value. We were the first large legal AI company to offer consumption-based pricing, so what a customer pays rises and falls with the work Legora does for them. We only grow with a customer when Legora is earning its place, which keeps our interests pointed the same way. It’s the rule we started with, written into how we charge. To keep earning that place, we do more than ship software. Building technology is hard. Changing how a law firm works is harder. So when we launched, we didn’t hand lawyers a product and wish them luck. We had former lawyers ready to sit with them and show how it fit their practice area. We call them legal engineers. We now employ more than 150, and they work inside customer teams on their hardest matters. One of them once flew from New York to Stockholm on a Saturday and spent a week and a half with our engineers. A large US firm wanted to switch to us, but needed one specific task solved, and we couldn’t do it yet. He built it. That is what we mean by partner. We now have more lawyers than software engineers. And daily active users now spend more than two hours a day on Legora. We started in Stockholm, where the whole Swedish legal market is smaller than one of the big New York firms, so the world was always our market. The US is now our largest market by revenue, and more than half of the AmLaw 50 are customers. We’re expanding globally across 18 offices. Yet, every new hire still onboards in Stockholm. blogs.content: Linklaters and Legora: building the firm-wide standard for agentic AI | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Resources Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Linklaters and Legora: building the firm-wide standard for agentic AI Linklaters and Legora: building the firm-wide standard for agentic AI Category published Oct 22, 2026 author Team Legora Over the past year, Linklaters, one of the world's largest law firms, has redefined its ways of working around the Legora Agent . The impact has been transformational. Within a month of rollout, 97% of weekly active users were working in the Agent. Combined, Linklaters' lawyers around the world have now spent over 35 years on the platform since deployment. Kris Sales, Product Owner for Legora, says, “I don't think we've ever had a technology product become so popular so quickly.” Kris has been involved with Legora since the very first conversations, through the proof of concept, the deployment, and now day-to-day operation. Alongside him, Tom Quoroll and Sarah Barnard sit at the centre of Linklaters' relationship with Legora. Together they steer the firm's AI strategy, work that covers everything from tool rollouts to the strategic questions AI raises about the firm’s business model and how it trains the lawyers of the future. As one of the world’s largest law firms, Linklaters is often engaged by clients on highly complex matters that span multiple legal jurisdictions. That means the opportunity to take advantage of the benefits of AI is a global one, and Legora has been rolled out across Linklaters’ firm-wide as a result, but it also makes the work around adoption and the partnership with technology providers even more important. In their roles, Tom and Sarah are thinking deeply about how AI is deployed and adopted effectively and responsibly across Linklaters, as well as assessing the granular matter level data to understand when and where AI is being used to deliver benefits – both areas where the partnership with Legora has paid dividends. On the frontline of client delivery, the pair also recently founded Applied Intelligence, a new practice group bringing data scientists and lawyers together under one roof to work on clients’ most complex problems. Sarah is Linklaters’ Director of AI Delivery, responsible for taking that strategy and transferring it into a credible working practice, with measurable growth to show for it month on month. As Tom puts it: “Between the three of us, you have the team required to transform a law firm. We're each bringing different parts of the puzzle.” The impact of the partnership Firm-wide weekly active use rose almost 15% since the Legora Agent was rolled out, against a user base that expanded faster still (growing by approximately 20%) as Legora was adopted more widely across the firm. Partner engagement strengthened over the same period: monthly active partners rose from 65% to almost 80%, which is one of the fastest partner adoption ramps either Linklaters or Legora has seen. Monthly adoption of the Legora Agent now stands at 70%. Working closely with Legora’s Legal Engineers, Tom, Sarah and Kris have turned a technology rollout into a genuine change in how the firm operates. Here’s how they achieved it. A peer-led approach to adoption When the Linklaters team started evaluating AI platforms, they had already worked through two rounds of AI tooling. This meant the firm went into the process focused less on demos and more on how the right platform would actually feel in a lawyer's hands. “We had quite a high bar to start from in some ways,” says Kris, “because our users knew what they wanted.” When Legora reached those users, the feedback came back fast. “It was a much simpler interface, they just got on with it better,” says Kris. blogs.content: Insights Which Provisions Need a Second Look in a Contract Risk Assessment? A contract risk assessment under deadline needs a shortlist. See how deal context sets counsel's order, how clauses interact, and what to read before signing. by Harvey Team • Nov 2, 2026 A contract risk assessment finds the terms in an agreement that could cost your organization money, data, or control, and decides what to do about each one. Contract risk analysis checklists and likelihood-and-impact matrices tell you which kinds of risk to look for. Under a deadline, counsel also has to decide which provisions in this contract, for this deal, get a second look first. Take a hypothetical request that lands at 3:00 p.m. on a Friday afternoon. The VP of Support wants the contract for an AI customer support platform signed by Monday, at $180,000 a year, billed annually in advance. The provider's paper comes in three parts: a master services agreement (MSA), an order form, and online terms the MSA pulls in by URL. The platform will read your support tickets, so it will hold your customers' names, email addresses, and order histories. We'll follow this request from Friday afternoon to Monday's signature. Harvey reviews all three documents first, and counsel uses those results to rank the provisions that need a second look and to check the final copy before signing. Harvey's First Pass Turns Three Documents Into Four Flags Against Your Playbook The three documents go through Contract Intelligence, Harvey's contract review AI . It checks each document against your team's standard positions, which Harvey can build from contracts you've already signed.Those positions live in your contract playbook , and clauses that no rule covers get flagged as well. In this example, four provisions come back flagged. The provider's right to train its models on customer data, its right to add subprocessors by updating a web page, and a 36-month auto-renewal each depart from your positions. The MSA's change-in-terms provision matches no rule at all, so it goes to counsel for manual review. It lets the provider update its online terms by posting them, and it makes those terms control in a conflict. Your playbook in this example accepts a 12-month cap for software subscriptions, so the provider's cap doesn't come back as a deviation. Counsel also checks precedent. In this example, two earlier AI tool agreements that process customer data closed with a separate, higher cap for data-protection breaches. In Practice: At Repsol , review of a single contractual clause used to take the compliance team 30 to 60 minutes. With Harvey, the team has cut that time by over 90%, typically to a few minutes. This In Practice episode shows how legal teams build and run Playbooks directly in Word, the kind of review the support platform's paper gets on Friday. Watch Video Counsel's Contract Risk Assessment Ranks Five Provisions by What This Deal Puts at Stake By 5:00 p.m., counsel orders a shortlist from the four flags, the precedent note, and what this deal puts at stake. The order is counsel's own call. Here's the shortlist counsel builds, with all provisions and positions hypothetical: Order Provision Why counsel ranks it here Deal context 1 The provider may use customer data to train its models (online terms) Data used in training is hard to claw back, so this is the hardest term to fix after signing Support tickets carry your customers' personal data, which brings in privacy review 2 The provider may update the online terms by posting them, and the online terms control in a conflict (MSA) No playbook rule covers it, and it can rewrite provisions 1 and 4 after signing The training right and the subprocessor terms both live in the online terms 3 A liability cap of 12 months' fees, with no separate cap for data breaches (MSA) It matches your standard, but it would limit recovery for a data breach to $180,000 The platform holds customer personal data, and two earlier AI tool deals got a data cap

blogs.content: Insights Three Ways AI Changes What Small Firms Can Take On Acevedo Belt’s experience with Harvey shows how small firms can use AI to pursue complex, time-sensitive matters while keeping senior lawyers focused on the analysis and advice clients need. by Harvey Team • Oct 30, 2026 A client asked Acevedo Belt , a Miami-based boutique firm with an all-senior attorney model, to complete initial investor due diligence on a nine-figure deal within 48 hours. Hundreds of closing documents needed to be reviewed and summarized, and last-minute changes raised questions that required quick analysis. For a small firm, the challenge was how to handle that volume while preserving time for the judgment the deal demanded. Acevedo Belt used Harvey to move through the document package, giving its attorneys more time to focus on substance, risk, and strategy. It met the client’s accelerated timeline. More broadly, Acevedo Belt’s experience points to an opportunity for small firms: AI can help them take on demanding, time-sensitive matters while senior lawyers remain responsible for interpreting the findings and advising clients on their significance. 1. Handle Document-Heavy Matters With a Lean Team A document-heavy transaction can require substantial time for review, research, and synthesis. Larger firms can spread those tasks across a larger team; a boutique has fewer people to assign. Acevedo Belt built its practice around senior attorneys handling complex matters, so simply adding more junior lawyers would mean a different model of practice. On the due diligence assignment, Harvey helped the team quickly synthesize the document package, giving attorneys a faster starting point for their review. That use was part of a broader approach: attorneys use Harvey for due diligence, drafting, document analysis, and synthesizing findings, with playbooks and agents built into the firm’s core workflows. The firm also created short videos and on-demand tutorials and held weekly “Tech Tuesdays” to share updates and work through questions. 2. Keep Senior Lawyers Focused on Judgment AI can help a small firm work through information more quickly, but clients still rely on lawyers to decide which details are important, how they affect a matter, and what advice to give. The added capacity is valuable when senior attorneys can apply their experience to those decisions. Brian Belt, Founding Partner at Acevedo Belt, says senior attorneys carefully verify work generated by Harvey, just as they do work from junior lawyers. Harvey’s footnotes make that review easier by letting attorneys trace statements back to source documents. They then assess what the findings mean for the matter and the advice the client needs. “ There is something deeply personal and inspirational about knowing that you have the time to dig deeper, to ask the questions you want to ask, and to generate your best work without compromise. It's made practicing law more fun and rewarding, and much less stressful. ” Brian Belt Founding Partner at Acevedo Belt 3. Put Time Savings Back Into Client Work For a small firm, time saved on repeatable tasks creates room to give clients more attention, pursue questions in greater depth, and produce stronger work. Acevedo Belt attorneys reported saving 10–50% of their time each week by using Harvey, depending on the user, practice area, and task. The firm says it put that time toward client work, deeper research, and improved work product. Its AI capabilities also helped it win new work: a client chose Acevedo Belt over another law firm for a substantial assignment, citing its use of AI-powered legal technology as the deciding factor. A global consultancy partner also referred a major client after repeatedly noting the firm’s use of AI. blogs.description: Harvey usage data shows how legal AI adoption is growing across seniority levels, practice areas, and markets, offering lessons for firms planning a rollout.
blogs.content: Insights What the Data Shows About Legal AI Adoption Harvey usage data shows how legal AI adoption is growing across seniority levels, practice areas, and markets, offering lessons for firms planning a rollout. by Katie Burke and John Haddock • Oct 30, 2026 Two years ago, the question most law firms asked about AI was whether to adopt it. Today, the questions we get surround how much, how fast, and at which levels organizations are adopting AI, so we thought it might be helpful to ground the discussion in data from our hundreds of thousands of users. Partners Represent Nearly a Quarter of Harvey’s Law Firm Users Let’s start with the most common misconception we hear about AI and legal, which is the trope that “only junior associates use AI.” The number of Harvey users who are partners is more than 4x what it was this time last year. Partners now represent 23% of Harvey’s law firm users, nearly a quarter. This is significant for a few reasons: not only are partners regularly using and seeing value with AI, but they are also helping set the tone for their organizations on responsible adoption of AI in their daily work. In addition to being clear from the data, we see this regularly in our customer feedback and discussions with law firms. At this year’s US Open, a very AI-savvy partner made the rounds to ask about the best agent their team was using regularly. This is not an accident — partners have moved from encouraging their associates to use AI and being open to experimentation and shifted into more daily usage and adoption by the senior partners within firms. The Tone on AI Starts at the Top The incentive for partners to use AI is not just their own work product and daily habits. When partners are more engaged, associates are notably more likely to use AI more frequently. Associate utilization rates were 25 points higher when Partner utilization was in the top quartile, which is one of the many reasons we highly encourage partners to join our adoption workshops and training in rollout planning. We met with a law firm that was considering Harvey who asked if it was okay if a few of the partners who participated in the pilot could share examples and use cases as part of the firm-wide rollout of Harvey. Not only is that welcome, it’s encouraged — there is no one who understands your organization better than the folks who work in it daily, so our approach to training and transformation is always to work deeply to earn and maintain the trust of your partners and your team. Practice Group Patterns Matter Among our law firm customers, Corporate (inclusive of M&A) has the highest query volume, followed by Litigation, Banking & Finance, and Real Estate. Some of this is directly correlated to early adopters of Harvey and to the transaction volume associated with their work, but we also see connectivity to how much partners see direct value from AI and set that example for their teams. Not to be left behind, the fastest growing practice groups by query volume include Litigation, Real Estate, Intellectual Property, and Family Law. Harvey data from June reflects more specificity, noting due diligence and deal management as common go-tos for corporate attorneys, while on the litigation side of the house, we see a lot of case management, regulatory and advisory analysis alongside discovery and trial preparation. The most common tasks we’re seeing with agents are drafting, analysis and review, and extracting information from documents. It’s exciting to see the patterns of how different practices are using Harvey, and just as fun to hear about new applications. For example, we’re hearing about how employment lawyers are using Harvey’s agentic capabilities and seeing how horizon scanning helps lawyers across practice areas prepare for legal and regulatory changes. blogs.title: Turning a Raw Deposition Transcript Into a Usable Record
blogs.author: Harvey Team
blogs.description: Learn how litigation teams turn deposition transcripts into source-linked, usable records for case strategy, drafting, and trial preparation.
blogs.content: Insights Turning a Raw Deposition Transcript Into a Usable Record Learn how litigation teams turn deposition transcripts into source-linked, usable records for case strategy, drafting, and trial preparation. by Harvey Team • Oct 29, 2026 By the time a deposition ends, a litigation team may have hundreds of pages of testimony and very little time to turn it into something useful. The transcript preserves what was said, but it doesn’t tell you which admissions matter, where a witness’s account shifted, which exhibits carry the point, or how the testimony fits with the rest of the record. An AI deposition summary can shorten that first pass. What’s more valuable is a working record organized around the issues in dispute, linked back to the underlying testimony, checked against the operative transcript, and structured for whatever the team needs to do next. A Deposition Transcript is the Record, but Not a Working Case Tool Depositions are organized in the order that questions were asked, not necessarily in the order a lawyer will later need the facts. Witnesses might discuss the same issue at several points, qualify an answer thirty pages later, or refer to an exhibit that only becomes important once another witness is deposed. A usable record reorganizes that testimony around the case. It should make it easy to see what the witness admitted or denied, where the account changed, what events belong on the chronology, which documents matter, and where the team needs to follow up. This way, the transcript remains the source of truth, while the working record makes it more efficient to use. Before Summarizing, Confirm Which Version of the Transcript You’re Working From Transcript analysis gets harder to trust when the team isn’t clear on which version sits underneath it. Before you summarize, extract, or compare testimony, identify whether you’re working from a rough transcript, a final transcript, or a version that’s been corrected. Distinguish a Rough Transcript From the Final Certified Record A rough transcript can be useful when the team needs to start analysis immediately after the deposition. Treat that work as provisional, though. Wording, formatting, and page-line references may change before the final certified transcript is available, so check quotations and pinpoint references again before using them in a filing, examination outline, or other work product. Incorporate Corrections and the Errata Sheet If the witness later makes permitted changes, those updates need to travel with the analysis. In federal practice, Rule 30(e) provides a process for reviewing the transcript or recording and listing changes and the reasons for them when review was requested before the deposition ended. Other jurisdictions may handle the process differently, but the practical point is the same. A summary created before an errata sheet or other correction is incorporated may no longer reflect the operative record. Preserve the Source Structure From the Beginning Keep the reference information that helps a lawyer get back to the testimony quickly. This typically includes page and line numbers, speaker, exhibit references, and any other useful transcript markers. Stripping those details out may make a summary look cleaner, but it also makes every important finding harder to verify and cite later. Choose the Deposition Summary Format Based on What the Team Needs to do Next No single deposition summary format works for every task. The right structure depends on the job the summary needs to support, and the same transcript may justify more than one output. Page-Line Summaries Make Precise Testimony Easier to Retrieve Use a page-line summary when the team expects to return to exact testimony often. These work especially well for impeachment preparation, motion drafting, witness outlines, and any task where the reader needs a concise description of the answer next to a clear and precise source reference. blogs.content: Insights Extending Legal Agent Bench to U.S. Case Law Introducing a new extension to Legal Agent Bench that tests frontier models’ ability to research and draft litigation briefs end-to-end using real case records. by Laura Toulme and Julio Pereyra • Oct 29, 2026 Today we introduce LAB: United States Case Law (LAB: USCL), an evaluation framework for testing frontier models’ ability to research and draft litigation briefs end-to-end using real case records. LAB: USCL adds novel approaches to LAB for understanding model behavior by building environments from real, public data collected by Free Law Project and evaluating model-written briefs head-to-head. We find that a small group of frontier models can now research and write complete, first-draft briefs in a single shot with no attorney guidance. While these briefs still exhibit a long tail of failure modes, they are substantially closer to the high bar for filing with a court and mark a substantial advance on a task that demands complex legal reasoning and advocacy. In this post we discuss our initial findings on these emerging capabilities as well as how we plan to make research in this area more accessible in partnership with Grubel. Brief Writing: An Ultra-Long Horizon Task When parties to a litigation want a court to act, they file a motion: a formal request asking the judge to issue a specific order or ruling. A motion may ask the court to do routine things like change a deadline or take more dramatic actions like dismissing a case or sanctioning a party. Some motions are opposed by the other parties, who argue that it would be legally incorrect or otherwise inappropriate for the court to take the requested action. To support these more contested motions, parties file briefs: written advocacy explaining why the court is justified in taking some action based on the state of the case, the law and precedent, and other considerations. Brief writing is one of the most complex tasks in litigation, sometimes requiring a team of lawyers multiple weeks to write and refine a compelling argument. An agent replicating this work must complete the same three steps a lawyer does: understanding the state of the case, researching the case law, and writing the brief itself. Understanding the State of the Case. For agents, the first part of replicating this work is understanding the state of the case by reviewing its docket, the official record of the case’s proceedings. The docket lists every filing, meaning every document submitted to the court, such as the complaint that starts the lawsuit, the motions and briefs that contain the parties’ arguments, and exhibits supporting those arguments, such as contracts, letters, or financial records. It also records the judge’s orders and rulings. In complex or long-running cases, the docket can span thousands of filings. Figure 1. A sample PACER docket with identifying details anonymized. A docket lists filings and court actions in chronological order, with hyperlinks to download the underlying documents. Researching Case Law. The next step is case law research: finding the past court decisions that bear on the legal questions in a case and determining how much weight each one carries. When judges rule on motions or decide cases, they often explain their reasoning in written opinions. Together, these opinions make up case law, the body of rules that comes from judges’ decisions, as opposed to rules passed by legislatures (statutes) or issued by agencies (regulations). These decisions carry weight because they create precedent. In the United States legal system, judges are expected to justify their decisions by relying on earlier opinions. Some of those opinions are binding: a court must follow decisions on the same legal question from higher courts in its jurisdiction. Other opinions, such as decisions from other trial courts, are only persuasive, so a court can look to them for guidance but doesn’t have to follow them. Case law research requires a

blogs.content: Insights ESI Protocol Best Practices for Search Terms and Production Format Before Discovery Starts Learn how to negotiate ESI protocol search terms, production formats, metadata, and change procedures before discovery begins. by Harvey Team • Oct 28, 2026 ESI protocol disputes rarely start with a disagreement about whether electronically stored information should be produced. Instead, the friction is typically over what gets searched, how the search is run, and whether the production arrives in a form counsel can actually use. These decisions are much easier to resolve before collection, review, and production are already in motion. In federal litigation, Rule 26(f) requires the parties’ discovery plan to address issues involving electronically stored information, including the form or forms of production. Rule 34 allows a requesting party to specify a production form and set defaults when no form has been agreed. An ESI protocol is one way to turn those obligations into practical rules for the matter, although the Federal Rules do not require every case to use a document with that title. However, timing matters — once a team has reviewed a large population under one search approach or begun producing data in an agreed format, changing course can create avoidable rework and new disputes. This guide focuses on two decisions worth settling early: search methodology and production format. For broader lifecycle context, see our eDiscovery guide for law firms . Key Takeaways: Negotiate the methodology, not just the keywords: A list of terms does not show how a search will be scoped, tested, or refined. Agreeing on the methodology upfront gives both sides a clearer basis for judging whether the search is reasonable and reduces the risk of expensive rework later. Test assumptions before they become protocol language: Hit counts alone cannot tell you whether a query is finding the right material or missing known responsive documents. Sampling and comparing results before the protocol is finalized can surface problems while the parties still have room to adjust. Choose production formats for how the evidence will be used: Native files, images, searchable text, and metadata preserve different kinds of context and functionality. Resolving those choices early makes the resulting production easier to review, analyze, cite, and defend. Build change into the protocol from the start: New custodians, data sources, terminology, or technical constraints often emerge after discovery begins. A defined process for revisiting search and production decisions keeps ordinary course corrections from turning into avoidable disputes. An ESI Protocol Should Resolve the Hard Choices Before the Data Starts Moving A useful ESI protocol reduces ambiguity before ambiguity becomes expensive. It should tell the parties enough about preservation, search, review mechanics, and production that each side understands the operating rules of discovery. It should also leave room for the facts to change. Keep in mind that this doesn’t mean that every case needs the same level of detail. A protocol for a focused contract dispute might look very different from one involving dozens of custodians, collaboration platforms, databases, and years of communications. The goal is not to reproduce a model order. It’s to identify the decisions that could materially affect scope, burden, usability, or later motion practice and resolve as many of them as practical at the outset. Courts may also expect counsel to address ESI early. For example, the Northern District of California’s ESI Guidelines and Checklist are meant to be consulted at the beginning of a case and specifically direct attention to preservation, search methodology, and production format. Local rules, standing orders, and judge-specific practices should therefore be part of the preparation, not an afterthought. Hooper • Oct 28, 2026 My path to Legal Engineering brought together several parts of my career that once seemed unrelated. I began as an Assistant District Attorney, carrying a full docket and trying misdemeanor and felony cases before juries. It taught me how to think on my feet, explain complicated issues clearly, and earn the confidence of people being asked to consider something unfamiliar. (Once you’ve stood in front of a jury during a complex trial, walking a room of partners or in-house counsel through a new technology feels a lot less intimidating.) From there I worked as a firm litigator, then a Program Attorney for the Colorado Bar Association CLE before moving in-house as Managing Counsel at Toyota Financial Services. As digital marketing became a larger part of my work, the questions increasingly extended beyond advertising into data, privacy, and the technology behind the campaigns. To better understand those issues, I earned certifications in data privacy and AI governance, including the CIPP/US and AIGP , and later earned a master’s degree in Technology Leadership at Brown University. Along the way, I watched technology change legal work faster than many organizations could establish the guardrails for using it. I became interested in the practical challenge of helping legal teams adopt AI responsibly: identifying where it could improve the work, translating legal processes into effective workflows, and determining where lawyers still needed to review and decide. As a Legal Engineer at Harvey, I found a role that brings those responsibilities together. “ Legal Engineers sit in the middle [of attorneys and technology], speak both languages, and turn a lawyer’s judgment into something the platform can execute reliably. ” Building AI Around How Lawyers Actually Work A Legal Engineer starts by understanding how a legal organization works: the task it is trying to complete, the standards it applies, and what useful work product looks like. From there, we help determine how Harvey can support that process, whether the team is reviewing contracts against a playbook, extracting key terms from hundreds of documents, drafting agreements, or conducting legal research. The work often moves quickly from understanding a problem to building a solution. I might begin by training a legal team on Harvey, then work alongside its lawyers to build and test a custom agent or review table using documents from an active matter. Behind the scenes, I work with other Legal Engineers to evaluate new product capabilities and determine how they could address the challenges we hear from customers. Recently, my colleagues and I spent two days with an in-house legal department, running training and advanced working sessions with teams across marketing, compliance, product, and other functions. Together, we built custom agents for tasks they had previously handled manually. We then helped the lawyers build their own agents and workflows, so they left with both practical solutions and the ability to continue developing new ones. “ The work is about amplifying attorney judgment, not removing it. Every agent and review table I build is designed so an attorney stays in the loop: reviewing, deciding, and owning the call. ” The hardest part of our sessions wasn’t building the technology. It was helping experienced lawyers put words to decisions they had made instinctively for years. They had to define which clauses they would flag, which facts would change their analysis, what acceptable language looked like, and whether an issue required further review. blogs.content: Insights Drafting a First Answer to a Complaint From Exemplars Learn how litigation teams can draft an answer to a complaint from firm exemplars, current matter facts, and verified sources with AI-assisted workflows. by Harvey Team • Oct 28, 2026 When a complaint lands, the real work is turning a new set of allegations into a defensible response under deadline, while making sure facts, procedural choices, and client strategy belong to this matter (not the last one). Most firms already have useful prior work, so a relevant answer from a similar case can show how the team structures responses, handles recurring allegations, and frames defenses. At the same time, it can also create risk if old facts, outdated law, or case-specific strategy carry over unnoticed. A better workflow starts with the current complaint, confirms the procedural posture, finds the right exemplars, drafts against verified matter facts, and then compares the result back to both the complaint and the precedent set. In this article, we’ll look at how AI can speed up the document-heavy parts of that process, while ensuring that counsel still owns the choices that affect the client's position. Before Drafting, Confirm That an Answer is the Right Response Before starting a draft, confirm that an answer is actually the next filing that the matter requires. In federal court, Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12 governs the timing of responsive pleadings and allows certain defenses to be raised by motion. State rules, local rules, standing orders, and case-specific deadlines can change the analysis. That matters because some procedural choices have sequencing consequences. In federal practice, Rule 12(b) motions generally must be made before the responsive pleading when a responsive pleading is allowed, while Rule 12(c) provides for judgment on the pleadings after the pleadings close. Drafting first and analyzing posture later can narrow options the team meant to preserve. Before drafting, we recommend confirming: The court, jurisdiction, and governing rules. The service date and response deadline, which in federal court, is generally 21 days after service of the summons and complaint to answer. If the defendant timely waives service, that period can be extended to 60 days after the waiver request was sent, but a Rule 12 motion can change the timeline as well (typically due 14 days after notice that the motion was denied). Whether counsel is evaluating a pre-answer motion or another response. The claims, parties, requested relief, and any responsive claims that require analysis. Any local rules, standing orders, or judge-specific requirements affecting form or timing. Those answers also define what makes a prior answer relevant. For example, an exemplar from the same court and claim type may be far more useful than a more recent filing from a different procedural setting. What a First Answer to a Complaint Needs to Accomplish Once the response path is clear, an answer has three core jobs: Respond to the allegations. State the defenses and other responsive claims counsel intends to assert. Comply with the filing requirements that apply to the case. The document may look familiar, but each of those jobs depends on the current record. Respond to the Complaint's Allegations In federal court, Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 8 requires a responding party to admit or deny the opposing party’s allegations and permits a statement of insufficient knowledge or information to operate as a denial. If only part of an allegation is true, the rule calls for admitting that part and denying the rest. That makes complaint parsing more than an administrative step. Each numbered allegation needs a deliberate response tied to the facts the team can support. A fluent paragraph copied from an exemplar is less useful than a structured map showing what’s admitted, denied, partly admitted, or still needs factual investigation. blogs.author: Vineet Shahani
blogs.description: The biggest delays in legal work often happen before review begins. Harvey’s Deputy General Counsel, Vineet Shahani, explains how a connected intake process can move legal work forward from the moment a request arrives.
blogs.content: Insights Why Legal Intake Should Create a Clear Path to Resolution The biggest delays in legal work often happen before review begins. Harvey’s Deputy General Counsel, Vineet Shahani, explains how a connected intake process can move legal work forward from the moment a request arrives. by Vineet Shahani • Oct 27, 2026 Requests to the legal team rarely arrive through one channel. A contract may come through email, a policy question through Slack, a marketing review through a design tool, and a product review may arrive by email with supporting documents in Google Drive. For the business, it can be difficult to know where to go for legal advice or who is the right lawyer for a particular request. Once a request reaches the legal team, they may need to follow up for missing context and find the relevant policies or precedents before review can begin. The team then identifies the right reviewer, reassigning the request if priorities or capacity change. Even for recurring requests, they may have to repeat these steps from scratch. A better intake model should move the request toward resolution from the moment it arrives. AI can support that process by helping gather the necessary context, applying the company’s legal standards, and directing each request to the appropriate member of the legal team, whether a contract manager, lawyer, or paralegal. Business teams get the guidance they need sooner, while lawyers spend less time coordinating and reviewing playbooks and precedents and more time applying their expertise. What Slows Legal Requests Down A request entering the legal team’s queue doesn’t necessarily mean it’s ready for review. A business stakeholder may know the outcome they need, but not the facts a lawyer needs to advise them. A customer’s marked-up MSA, for example, may arrive without the deal value, signing deadline, or context on what the parties have already discussed. The legal team then has to fill in the gaps by following up with the requester, locating the relevant documents and internal guidance, and determining who should handle the review. Even assigning the request can require coordination. The usual reviewer may be unavailable or at capacity, leaving someone to identify an alternative and transfer the context. By the time the request reaches the right person with the necessary information, days can pass. In the meantime, the business may move ahead or make commitments that leave the legal team with less room to advise. What appears to be a slow legal review is often just time spent preparing the request for legal review. This administrative burden becomes harder to sustain as demand for legal support grows without a corresponding increase in resources. In RSGI’s recent research , 68% of in-house legal teams expect their headcount to remain flat over the next year. Yet 92% of respondents reported faster turnaround of legal work to the business after adopting Harvey. That result points to how AI can help legal teams respond to business needs more quickly within existing capacity. Different Requests Need Different Paths Reducing time-consuming administrative work starts with recognizing that legal requests are not interchangeable. A marketing asset review may require details about the audience, claims, and supporting evidence before the legal team returns marked-up copy. A product review may involve a PRD, rollout plans, and input from several specialists before the business receives guidance on whether it can launch. Each request requires different context, expertise, and approvals. A fixed intake process struggles to account for those differences. If it asks too little, the legal team still has to gather the missing context. If it asks every possible question upfront, the process becomes burdensome and business users may avoid it. The intake experience should adapt to the work , gathering the information required for that request and directing it through the appropriate review process. Design Intake Around how

blogs.description: Spellbook Labs analyzed 3,000+ public-company agreements across 520 organizations. Sixty percent had drafting errors.
blogs.content: 60% of SEC-Filed Contracts Contain Errors | Spellbook Labs spellbook.legal cookie bridge --> Overview Findings at a Glance Issues by Company Issues by Founding Decade Issues by Industry Issues by Contract Type Issues by Filing Year Conclusion Methodology and Scope Humans Hallucinate Too Humans Hallucinate Too. 60% of SEC-Filed Contracts Contain Errors Spellbook Labs analyzed 60,000 pages of public-company agreements across 520 organizations. Sixty percent of contracts had drafting errors. When a self-driving car crashes, it makes the news. The scrutiny is warranted, but the headlines obscure the baseline. Human drivers cause far more crashes . They happen every day, yet almost none become media stories. In legal work, AI hallucinations also get the headlines. An AI-generated legal brief citing non-existent case studies. A judge who used AI to create a restraining order and misquoted state law. These are real issues that deserve attention. But Spellbook sees a different side to AI’s impact on legal and contract workflow. We see the human mistakes that are made when volume and complexity are met with limited hours and manual review. In fact, our data shows saved hours, greater accuracy and increased output when AI is deployed. So we decided to dig into the data to prove what we already know intuitively—humans make mistakes too. Using Spellbook Reviews, we analyzed 3,000+ SEC-filed contracts from over 500 companies, spanning 22 years. These were executed agreements from some of the largest and most heavily lawyered companies in the world. The findings showed plenty of interesting trends and fun examples. Six in ten contracts contained drafting issues. Many were minor. But one in 40 was high-risk—defined as changing the meaning of an agreement in a substantially negative way for at least one party—and they were concentrated in provisions that decide who gets paid, who carries the liability, and what happens in a dispute. None of this is a matter of carelessness by lawyers so much as a consequence of the length, complexity, and disjointed nature of how these types of SEC-filed agreements are prepared and negotiated. In this context, mistakes are inevitable. But they don’t have to be. Every company, public or private, will eventually run its contracts through products like Spellbook that will not only spot errors and risks immediately but suggest fixes based on a company’s own agreement context and real-time market data. Issue Example: A loan cap written two different ways. A mining company's loan agreement set its borrowing limit at "One Million Five-Hundred Sixty Thousand Dollars," then printed the figure beside it as $1,750,000.00. The words and the number differ by $190,000, and the mismatch appears twice. If the borrower and lender ever disagree, the contract gives a court no clear answer, and $190,000 turns on who wins. Findings at a Glance This study should be treated as a proxy for how much humans miss. We kept our analysis deliberately narrow, counting only objective drafting mistakes we could verify from the document itself. We could not judge whether an agreement was signed out of policy, drifted off market, or if a company gave away more than it should, let alone what sits inside the millions of private contracts. These numbers should be thought of as the floor, not a full account of everything worth fixing in an agreement. blogs.content: Insights How AI Helps Employment Legal Teams Handle Contracts, Disputes, and Investigations See how employment legal teams use AI to draft and review documents, investigate workplace issues, analyze disputes, and reuse trusted legal knowledge. by Harvey Team • Oct 26, 2026 Employment legal work rarely arrives as one kind of task. A team might review an offer letter in the morning, answer a handbook question before lunch, then open an employee complaint that later becomes an agency charge or litigation. The work changes, but the underlying burden is similar: find the right facts, compare them with company standards and applicable law, and turn that context into something counsel can review and act on. This is where legal AI is most useful because it can take a first pass on document-heavy work like drafting from approved precedent, structuring a complaint, building a chronology, comparing statements, or summarizing a demand letter. Lawyers still own credibility calls, risk tolerance, negotiation posture, and legal strategy. This article isn’t about automated systems used to screen candidates or make employment decisions. For in-house legal teams , the larger opportunity is primarily around connecting contracts, investigations, disputes, and institutional knowledge in one system instead of treating each task as a separate AI use case. Use AI to Draft and Review Employment Documents More Consistently Employment documents are repeatable, but they aren’t static. Offer letters, employment agreements, releases, handbooks, and disciplinary notices all need to reflect the organization’s current positions and the rules that apply in the relevant jurisdiction. Start First Drafts From Approved Templates and Precedent The best starting point is usually material your team already trusts. An AI draft based on an approved template, a prior agreement, and current instructions is more useful than one generated from a blank prompt because its starting point is already much closer to your organization’s actual standards. For example, counsel can use AI to prepare a first pass of an offer letter, employment agreement, separation agreement, NDA, or disciplinary notice, then review the terms that require judgment. Within Harvey, lawyers can also draft and edit in Word using precedents and source material from Vault or connected systems . For more information, our employment contract drafting guide dives deeper into the clause and jurisdiction decisions that employment teams need to make. Review Changes Against Your Standards For many teams, review matters more than generation. A counterparty redline, revised separation agreement, or updated form can be compared against approved positions to flag deviations, missing terms, and language that deserves a closer look. The lawyer then decides whether the change is acceptable, needs fallback language, or should be escalated. For repeatable review work, Contract Intelligence can review agreements against playbooks and precedent, surface deviations, and keep the review moving without turning approval into an automated decision. Interested in learning more about this stage of the process? Our guide to AI employment contract review covers what to check and what to flag in more detail. Keep Handbooks and Policies Aligned as Requirements Change Policies can also lead to a different maintenance problem. Your team may need to compare handbook language across jurisdictions, summarize a legal development for HR, identify inconsistencies between global and local policies, or draft revised language after a gap is found. AI can speed that analysis, but the output still needs a source trail and legal review. Harvey’s knowledge sources bring trusted legal sources together with your organization’s own knowledge and expertise, so counsel can research the relevant issue and then apply that analysis to the policy or handbook in front of them. blogs.description: Faster legal work raises a bigger question for firms: How can they turn time saved into better outcomes for their clients?
blogs.content: Insights How Law Firms Turn AI Efficiency Into Client Value Faster legal work raises a bigger question for firms: How can they turn time saved into better outcomes for their clients? by Harvey Team • Oct 23, 2026 AI is changing how quickly law firms can complete legal work. For clients, though, it’s about what that speed makes possible: an earlier business decision, a broader view of risk, or more time for the judgment a matter requires. At Harvey FORUM in Sydney, Hilary Goodier (Partner and Global Chair of NewLaw and Consulting at Ashurst Perkins Coie) and Michelle Mahoney (Chief Innovation Officer at Mallesons) were joined by Michael Griffith (Deputy General Counsel at Telstra) for a candid discussion of how AI is changing the value firms can deliver, and how clients assess it. Their perspectives offer a way for law firms and legal teams to think more clearly about pricing, service, and the time lawyers spend on the work that is more valuable. Show Clients What AI Changes Clients want to see what a firm’s use of AI changes about the work they receive. Griffith said Telstra, Australia’s leading telecommunications and information services company, evaluates firms on the same things it valued before AI — what has changed is the range of benefits a firm might be able to deliver. Watch Video His questions give firms a useful starting point when discussing a matter with a client. Could AI reduce the cost of the work? Help the firm deliver specialized advice sooner? Make it possible to examine more documents or identify risks that would otherwise go unexplored? The answer will depend on what the client is trying to achieve. A deadline tied to a business decision, for example, may make speed more valuable than a reduction in fees. That distinction is important when firms decide how to scope and price the work. The most compelling proposal is one that explains what the client will gain and how the firm plans to deliver it. Connect Faster Work to Client Value The value of faster work depends on what clients can do with the time gained. Goodier described an obligations mapping project for a global investment bank that her team completed in five weeks using AI, compared with an estimated six months by conventional methods. The client estimated that the work would allow it to enter a new market five months earlier. Watch Video Goodier said the firm spoke openly with the client about what the project needed to achieve and how to share the value created by using AI. In this case, the earlier market entry mattered more than the reduction in legal fees. On another matter, lower costs or a more thorough review might be the priority. Those differences are hard to reflect in a standard discount applied to every AI-assisted task. They also raise a question for firms built around billable hours. When a firm can deliver valuable work in much less time, an hourly fee may no longer reflect what the client receives or what it takes the firm to deliver it. Watch Video Changing the price is only part of the challenge. Goodier noted that targets and bonuses tied to hours can discourage lawyers from using methods that save time. Firms need to consider how they recognize that work internally if they want lawyers to deliver using AI consistently. Make Room for Deeper Analysis AI can also change the scope of the work a firm is able to offer. Mahoney described how her team now spends less time gathering and organizing data, leaving more time to examine what it reveals. Watch Video When lawyers spend less time gathering the data, they can examine more of it and ask questions that a narrower review might miss. Mahoney gave the example of examining a clause across thousands of arrangements, rather than looking at a small sample. Goodier pointed to contract remediation, portfolio reviews, and compliance projects that clients may previously have considered too expensive or time-consuming to pursue. blogs.title: What Does a Regulator Look for in Your Notice of Violation Response?
blogs.author: Harvey Team
blogs.description: What regulators look for in a notice of violation response, from FDA Form 483s to OSHA citations and Wells notices, and how to build the record first.
blogs.content: Insights What Does a Regulator Look for in Your Notice of Violation Response? What regulators look for in a notice of violation response, from FDA Form 483s to OSHA citations and Wells notices, and how to build the record first. by Harvey Team • Oct 22, 2026 A regulatory notice of violation means a regulator has looked at an organization's operations, practices, or conduct and found a potential compliance problem. Depending on the procedure, the organization may need to contest the finding, state its position, describe corrective actions taken or planned, or respond within a set period. The same phrase shows up on parking tickets and local code citations, but a regulatory finding needs its own response discipline. If your team is still interpreting new rules, regulatory change management comes first. This article walks through what starts after that work has run and a regulator has still found something. AI speeds up the first stage of the response. Harvey, for example, can help build the chronology and evidence index, test the finding against the record, and draft the first response pack. Your team spends its time on the position instead of on assembling the file. In the US, findings come from regulators such as the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA). The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and transportation security and nuclear regulators issue them, too. Elsewhere, a finding can arrive as a tax authority inquiry or a notice to produce from a workplace regulator. The document differs, but the response discipline stays the same. Examples of regulatory notices include: Notice Who Issues it What the Response Usually Involves FDA Form 483 FDA investigators, at the close of an inspection A voluntary written response, recommended within 15 business days, addressing each observation and any corrective actions taken or planned OSHA citation OSHA A written notice of contest within 15 working days if the employer contests. An informal conference can be requested in that window, but it doesn't extend the deadline SEC Wells notice SEC enforcement staff An optional Wells submission, written or by video, arguing why the Commission should not bring an action. The SEC ordinarily allows four weeks EPA notice of violation EPA A written response and corrective steps, with terms set by the statute involved While the procedures differ, every response has to hold up to an adversarial reader, match the record behind it, and survive the commitments it makes. The Response is Read Adversarially A response to a regulatory finding is a formal submission, and the regulator reads it against the facts already on record. Reviewers look for omitted information, statements that don't match the documents, and characterizations that flatter the facts beyond what the evidence supports. While you prepare the response, keep three things distinct: The response and its commitments. This is the formal submission, setting out the organization's position on the finding and any remediation it commits to. The factual record. These are the documents and other evidence that establish what happened and support each factual assertion in the response. Internal deliberations and legal analysis. These shape how the organization evaluates the finding. Depending on how particular communications were created and shared, attorney-client privilege or work-product protection may apply, so counsel should assess privilege and waiver before anything is disclosed. Whether a response or the material behind it can later be obtained, admitted, or used elsewhere depends on the regulator, the procedure, the jurisdiction, and the protections that apply. Every factual assertion needs a source in the file, and dates have to reconcile across the correspondence, the supporting documents, and the final submission. blogs.title: How We Made Review Tables Faster and More Reliable
blogs.author: Shrihari Murlidharan
blogs.description: Harvey engineers redesigned Review Table loading for reviews spanning thousands of documents, fetching rows page by page so large tables open faster and stay responsive.
blogs.content: Technical How We Made Review Tables Faster and More Reliable Harvey engineers redesigned Review Table loading for reviews spanning thousands of documents, fetching rows page by page so large tables open faster and stay responsive. by Shrihari Murlidharan and Stella Ge • Oct 22, 2026 The Review Table is Harvey’s largest, most exhaustive inference engine, allowing users to analyze thousands of legal documents and standardize insights using natural language. Lawyers can ask questions against uploaded documents and obtain the results in a structured tabular format, with rows corresponding to individual documents and columns mapping to the questions. Each cell answer includes the model’s reasoning and is backed by citations from the source document. Review Tables are also designed to be a living, collaborative surface: rows can be assigned out to collaborators for review, answers can be verified or locked, and users can leave comments for further discussion. Once verified, teams can lean on their review table as a reusable, validated source of truth for their next memo or presentation without needing to recreate their insights from scratch. That collaborative workflow depends on the table remaining responsive as it grows. As teams began querying hundreds of columns across thousands of files, loading the full table in the browser caused delays and, in the largest cases, could prevent it from loading at all. This post explains how we changed the table’s data and loading paths to support larger reviews while preserving sorting and filtering. When Browser Loading Hit its Limits Historically, all table operations were performed on the client side. The browser loaded the entire Review Table from the blob store and performed sorting, filtering, and any sort of aggregation in-memory. While this solution worked for small Review Tables, we saw performance issues once the table exceeded thousands of rows. When Review Tables adoption and usage skyrocketed, we saw that tables sometimes experienced lag times or became unresponsive. For extremely large tables, browsers could potentially run out of memory or fail to load entirely. It may seem like solving this scaling problem is straightforward. Since it’s a table data structure at its core, we should be able to address this problem by implementing server-side pagination. In reality, there’s two main things that prevent this fix: The requirement to segregate sensitive data . Client data at Harvey is extremely sensitive and as such, only the metadata lives in Postgres while raw customer data lives in Azure blobs. The data had to be fetched from Azure at request time, merged with Postgres data, and passed from the backend to the client. In order to support server-side pagination with filtering and sorting, we would need an interface to query on top of Azure blob store. There is no existing grid library that supports the kind of pagination scheme this would require . As a result, we had to come up with our own abstractions for page loading strategy, factoring in grouping by folder path, sorting, and filtering. In order to ensure this implementation achieved parity with our existing features, we built our own versions of table functionality for row selection and expanding/collapsing sections that we no longer got for free from our current grid library. How We Implemented Pagination Choosing a data store In order to scale the user interface, we moved all client side operations to the server side. This necessitated a reliable data store that both satisfied our segregation requirements and exposed a rich querying interface with aggregation. Postgres would still be our source of truth while the new data store would provide the read interface (CQRS pattern). Turbopuffer is a vector data store that runs on top of existing Azure blobs while supporting vector search (ANN, KNN), full text search (BM25), and straightforward filtering through an inverted index. blogs.content: Insights How AI is Expanding Legal’s Role Across the Business From advising on decisions earlier to building legal guidance into everyday workflows, Harvey Innovation Partner Dominic Ferullo explores how AI is impacting Legal’s contribution. by Dominic Ferullo • Oct 22, 2026 When I managed an in-house rollout of Harvey at NBCUniversal, I had two workflow imperatives: how could AI help our legal team get involved earlier in business decisions and how could we make our legal guidance easier for teams across the company to use? For us, that might’ve meant being brought into the creative and dealmaking processes that drive the entertainment industry. Now, as an Innovation Partner at Harvey, those same imperatives are front of mind for legal teams I work with across many industries. Legal teams are balancing a steady flow of requests with the need to advise while business decisions are still taking shape. AI can take on parts of high-volume work such as first-pass review, redlines, research, and regulatory monitoring, giving lawyers more room for judgment-heavy advice. The choices leaders make about that added capacity, including where Legal gets involved, what work it takes on, and how its guidance reaches colleagues, shape how the function contributes across the company. That contribution also often includes helping the company decide how to adopt AI more broadly. As AI moves into more functions, legal leaders are increasingly asked to guide rollout, governance, and measurement. Their experience applying AI within Legal gives them a practical perspective to bring to those decisions. Put New Capacity to Work When legal teams use AI, faster turnaround is often the first result the business notices. RSGI’s latest report , based on a survey of 25 in-house Harvey customers, found that 92% of respondents reported faster turnaround to the business. The same survey found that 88% of respondents said they spend more time with the business on higher-value work. Legal teams can direct that time toward judgment-heavy advice, bring more work in-house, and make approved guidance available for recurring questions. The right path depends on where Legal’s expertise can have the greatest impact. One financial services legal team in RSGI’s research used time freed through Harvey to advise on entering new markets and launching new products. At Repsol , the legal team completed a mid-sized M&A transaction in-house using Harvey; outside counsel quotes for the work averaged €200,000. From Individual Use to Business Workflows In my work with Harvey customers, I see adoption move through three stages. It often begins with individual legal professionals using AI for familiar tasks such as reviewing contracts against a playbook, researching a legal question, or preparing a first draft. As they find useful, repeatable applications, they can bring them into shared workflows within the legal department. This gives the legal team a consistent way to handle similar matters, even when different people are doing the work, and clarify where legal professionals need to review AI’s output. The broader shift comes when Legal connects its workflows to the places where other teams handle recurring work. With Harvey, legal teams can make approved guidance available through Spaces and Playbooks, so teams like Finance or Procurement can check routine work against Legal’s guardrails. Standard matters can move forward within those guardrails, while exceptions return to Legal for review. At Carrefour Spain , the legal team created self-service tools to help business colleagues generate certain contracts and answer common legal questions. Colleagues get a faster path through standard matters, while Legal has more time for questions that benefit from legal judgment.
